description: Alliance Gator Maxx G2 is the best polymeric sand for most paver patios. 6 picks sorted by joint width, from tight paver gaps to 4-inch flagstone joints.
dek: Alliance Gator Maxx G2 is the best polymeric sand for most paver patios.
intro: The best polymeric sand for a typical concrete or clay paver patio is Alliance Gator Maxx G2, because it is stocked almost everywhere, sets firmly and forgives the small watering slips first-timers make. If your pavers are smooth, light or already sealed, Techniseal HP NextGel is worth the step up because it is built to leave less haze on the faces.

Brand matters less than fit, though. Every bag is rated for a joint width range, and most failed jobs are a fine paver sand pushed into a flagstone gap or a coarse stone binder forced into a hairline paver joint. Below are six picks sorted by the joints they suit, then the questions that decide which bag you should actually buy.
quickAnswer: Measure your joints before you shop. For standard paver joints up to about 1/2 inch, buy Gator Maxx G2, or HP NextGel on smooth and light pavers. For flagstone and fieldstone gaps of 1 to 4 inches, skip paver sand and use a wide-joint binder such as Alliance GatorDust or Techniseal RG+.

blocks.p: Polymeric sands split into two families. Fine paver sands fill the narrow gaps between concrete and clay pavers. Coarse wide-joint binders fill the irregular, inches-wide gaps between natural stones. A great product from one family fails in the other, so the first decision is the family, and only then the brand.

Within the paver family, the real differences are how forgiving the binder is when you water it, how much haze it tends to leave, and where you can buy more if you run short. Those three points drive the ranking below. If you are still deciding whether to use a binder at all, read [polymeric sand vs regular sand for pavers](/polymeric-sand-vs-regular-sand-for-pavers/) first.

sections.h: The 6 Best Polymeric Sands in 2026, Ranked

blocks.p: This ranking leans on what each maker prints on the bag and data sheet (joint width range, minimum joint depth, rain and traffic windows) plus patterns that repeat in owner reviews. It is not based on field trials of our own, and where a maker does not publish a figure, it is left out.

blocks.h3: Best Overall: Alliance Gator Maxx G2

blocks.p: Gator Maxx G2 earns the top spot for a practical reason: when you are halfway through a patio and need two more bags of the same color, a landscape yard or home center near you probably has them. Alliance sells it for interlocking concrete and clay pavers with conventional joints, and the bag lists a width range in paver territory rather than the multi-inch gaps of flagstone. Owners commonly describe a firm, even set after one patient misting cycle, and joints that shrug off rain and hose spray once cured. Haze complaints are rare when the surface is blown completely clean before water goes on, though tumbled and textured pavers need extra passes with the blower. Colors include beige, slate grey and black, which cover most paver palettes. It is not the cheapest bag on the shelf, but it is the one least likely to surprise a first-time installer. Read the printed directions before you start; the watering sequence is specific to this formula.
**Pros:** easy to find in matching color lots; tolerant of minor watering mistakes; several colors; firm set that resists washout on gentle slopes.
**Cons:** made for paver joints, not wide flagstone gaps; still needs bone-dry pavers and a dry forecast; can haze on textured faces if dust is left behind.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Alliance+Gator+Maxx+G2+polymeric+sand&tag=sktiger-20)

Techniseal designed the NextGel line around the most common complaint about polymeric sand, a cloudy film left on the pavers after watering. Rather than a binder that dries as a residue wherever water carries it, the formula is designed to gel inside the joint, so less of it ends up smeared across the paver faces. That matters most on smooth, light-colored or already-sealed pavers, where any haze is obvious and stripping it means another product and another weekend. Techniseal also promotes the line as more tolerant of rain soon after installation than older sands; check the current bag for the exact window rather than assuming one. It is aimed at concrete pavers and some natural stone with joints in the paver range. Owners commonly report a joint that is hard on top with a slight give, which suits bases that shift a little between seasons. Expect to pay near the top of the category for it, and expect narrower shelf availability than Gator in some regions.
**Pros:** built specifically to cut surface haze; gels in the joint instead of filming the faces; good on smooth, light or pre-sealed pavers; firm but slightly flexible joint.
**Cons:** priced at the top of the category; harder to find than Gator in some areas; not for very wide stone joints.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Techniseal+HP+NextGel+polymeric+sand&tag=sktiger-20)

GatorDust is not a fine paver sand at all. It is a coarser, stone-dust style binder that Alliance designs for flagstone, bluestone, fieldstone and other natural stone laid with wide joints, and its label range runs to several inches of joint width instead of fractions of an inch. The coarse grading is the point: fine sand asked to bridge a 2-inch gap tends to shrink, split down the middle and wash out after a few storms, while a stone-dust blend packs into a stable mass. The cured joint is firm but a little softer than paver sand, which suits irregular flagging on a compacted aggregate base that moves slightly with the seasons. Colors are limited to a few earth tones that read naturally against stone. Plan your order carefully, because a wide, deep joint swallows material and one bag covers far less area than it would on pavers. Do not use it in tight concrete paver joints; it will not pack down into them.
**Pros:** coarse blend made to bridge wide joints; label range runs to multiple inches; slightly softer set tolerates seasonal movement; natural earth tones.
**Cons:** will not pack into narrow paver joints; wide joints use bags quickly; fewer colors than paver sands.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Alliance+GatorDust+stone+dust&tag=sktiger-20)

RG+ is Techniseal's product for joints too wide for its paver sands. The grain is coarser, and the company positions it for natural stone and flagstone with gaps well beyond what a standard polymeric sand can span. The practical reason to pick it over GatorDust usually comes down to your local supplier: many stone yards carry one brand family, and staying within one family keeps the cleaners, haze removers and instructions consistent if you also use Techniseal sand or sealer elsewhere on the property. RG+ handles irregular joints across one installation, which suits random flagstone where gaps run from a finger width to several inches. Like any wide-joint binder, it rewards a well-compacted base and joints that are clean and dry all the way down. Check the current label for the exact width range and minimum depth before you buy, and budget for more bags than a paver job of the same footprint.
**Pros:** formulated for wide joints and natural stone; coarser grain than Techniseal's paver sands; handles varied gap widths in one job; good fit where Techniseal is the dealer brand.
**Cons:** less common at big-box stores than GatorDust; limited color range; overkill in standard paver joints.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Techniseal+RG%2B+polymeric+sand&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best for Home Delivery: DOMINATOR Polymeric Sand

blocks.p: DOMINATOR sells mainly online, and that cuts both ways. If you live far from a landscape yard, or you are topping up joints on a small patio and do not want to haul heavy bags, having sand arrive at the door is genuinely handy. The company markets the formula as low-haze and pitches it for paver joints, with colors for grey, tan and charcoal pavers. The trade-off is cost per pound once shipping is built in, which can land well above a local Gator or Techniseal bag, and there is no store counter to walk back to if something goes wrong. Owners commonly report a firm set when the surface is cleaned well before misting, and the failures they describe trace back to damp pavers or too much water, the same as with every other brand. That answers the common question of DOMINATOR versus Techniseal: both work in paver joints, and the deciding factor is usually price per pound delivered and how much haze risk your pavers can tolerate. For multi-inch flagstone gaps, choose a dedicated wide-joint binder instead.
**Pros:** ships to the door; marketed as low-haze; several colors; detailed instructions online.
**Cons:** shipping pushes up the per-pound cost; less local support; not for very wide stone joints.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=DOMINATOR+polymeric+sand&tag=sktiger-20)

blocks.h3: Best Budget: Quikrete PowerLoc Jointing Sand

blocks.p: PowerLoc is the polymeric sand you will find in nearly every big-box garden aisle, usually at a lower shelf price than the landscape-yard brands. For a small backyard patio, a garden path or a few square feet of repair, it does the core job: the binder locks the joint, discourages weeds from rooting in the gap and stops the slow sand loss that plain joint sand suffers in heavy rain. Where it gives ground is tolerance. Owners commonly report that PowerLoc is less forgiving of over-watering, so flooding a section can carry binder out of the joint or onto the paver faces, leaving a soft joint, haze or both. Follow the bag's misting sequence closely and work in small sections. Color choices are fewer than Gator or Techniseal offer. On a large patio or a driveway, the premium for a more forgiving formula is usually money well spent, but for a weekend repair on a short path, PowerLoc is a sensible buy.
**Pros:** usually the cheapest name-brand bag in big-box stores; easy to find on short notice; fine for small patios and walks; neutral and grey colors.
**Cons:** less forgiving of over-watering; narrower color range; not for wide flagstone joints.
[Check price on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/s?k=Quikrete+PowerLoc+jointing+sand&tag=sktiger-20)

sections.h: How Do You Choose Polymeric Sand by Joint Width?

blocks.p: Measure before you compare brands. Check the narrowest and widest gaps across the whole area with a tape, then push a screwdriver into a few joints until it stops on bedding sand or base to find the depth. Every bag prints a width range and usually a minimum depth, and buying outside those numbers is the most common reason a job fails within a year.

blocks.h3: Depth matters as much as width

blocks.p: Most makers want the polymeric layer at least 1 to 1.5 inches deep so the binder has enough body to hold, and many say to fill the full paver depth. Thin pavers on a mortar bed, or tiles over a slab, leave joints too shallow for any polymeric sand. Those rigid installations need mortar or grout instead, and a [grout sealer](/best-grout-sealer/) afterward if the joints are cement-based.

If a paver patio runs into a flagstone path, buy two products and keep a border between them. Wide-joint binder in paver joints leaves voids; paver sand in flagstone joints cracks down the center. A second bag type costs little compared with redoing the whole surface.

sections.h: What Is the Best Polymeric Sand for Pavers?

blocks.p: For standard concrete pavers, Gator Maxx G2 is the safest pick and HP NextGel is the upgrade when haze would be hard to live with. Concrete pavers are dense and uniform, they sit on compacted gravel and an inch of bedding sand, and that is exactly the system polymeric sand was designed for. Any reputable paver sand works if the joints fall inside its range.

The finish of the paver decides how much haze risk you can accept. A dark, textured paver hides a faint polymer film. A smooth buff or white paver, or one that was sealed at the factory or by a previous owner, shows every smear. That is where a gel-type, low-haze sand pays for itself.

Clay brick behaves much like concrete pavers, but older brick can be thirsty. Wet a spare brick, let it dry, and watch how fast it darkens. If it drinks water quickly, choose a low-haze sand and spend extra time with the leaf blower before watering.

Driveways see turning tires and heavier loads, so compaction and joint depth matter even more. Fill joints to full depth, run a plate compactor with a urethane pad, and keep vehicles off for the full window on the bag, often 48 hours or more. Sealing the pavers later with a joint-stabilizing film from our [paver sealer picks](/best-paver-sealer/) helps the joints shed water and tire scuffing.

sections.h: What Is the Best Polymeric Sand for Flagstone and Natural Stone?

blocks.p: For flagstone, use a wide-joint binder: Alliance GatorDust first, Techniseal RG+ where that brand is easier to buy. Natural stone joints are usually wider and far less even than paver joints, which pushes past the range of fine sands.

Some sandstones and limestones absorb binder residue and show a darker outline along the joint. Test a spare stone or a hidden corner, and make sure the stone surface is completely dry before you spread anything. If the stone is sealed afterward, our [silane vs siloxane sealer guide](/silane-vs-siloxane-sealers/) explains which penetrating chemistry suits porous stone.

Porcelain is the opposite problem. It absorbs almost nothing, so any binder left on the surface sits there as a visible film. Pick a low-haze formula, blow the surface spotless and mist lightly. Some makers sell jointing products specifically for porcelain, and porcelain is often laid in thinner profiles, so confirm the joint depth meets the sand's minimum.
Never put polymeric sand in a permeable paver system. Those joints are meant to stay open and are filled with clean chip stone so rainwater can drain straight through to a stone reservoir below.

sections.h: How Many Bags of Polymeric Sand Do You Need?

blocks.p: Coverage depends on joint width, joint depth and paver size. Smaller pavers mean more joint length per square foot, so a cobble patio can use twice the sand of a slab patio with identical gaps. That is why every label gives a range rather than one number.

Treat those figures as planning ranges. Check the maker's coverage chart for your paver size, then add about 10 percent for spills and joints that swallow more than expected. A 300 square foot patio of standard pavers usually needs three to five bags; the same footprint in random flagstone can need 15 to 30.

blocks.h3: A quick field test for flagstone

blocks.p: Because flagstone gaps vary so much, fill a 10 square foot test patch, note how much it took, and multiply. Most suppliers take back unopened bags, so buying a margin is cheap insurance against finishing with a different color lot.

Keep bags off concrete floors and under cover. A bag that pulls in moisture can start to activate inside, forming stiff lumps that will not spread or pack. Return a clumped bag rather than breaking it up.

sections.h: Which Polymeric Sand Leaves the Least Haze?

blocks.p: Gel-activated formulas such as Techniseal HP NextGel are designed to leave the least haze, and DOMINATOR markets its formula the same way. But haze is mostly an installation problem, not a brand problem, and any sand will film the pavers if the conditions are wrong.

Polymer haze is binder that dried on the paver face instead of inside the joint. The three usual causes are fine dust left on the surface before watering, damp pavers during spreading, and too much water lifting binder up and over the joint edges.

blocks.h3: How to avoid it with any brand

ul: Start only on pavers that are dry to the bottom of the joints.
Sweep, then blow the surface with a leaf blower held low until no dust shows when you look across it toward the light.
Mist in light passes on a shower setting, never a jet.
Blow standing water off the faces after the last pass.

blocks.p: The full sequence, with timing, is in our [step-by-step polymeric sand guide](/how-to-use-polymeric-sand/).

Light haze often fades with weather over a few months. Heavier haze needs a polymer haze remover from the sand maker, used exactly as labeled and tested on a hidden spot first, since some removers can lighten concrete or affect sealer. Pressure washing alone rarely clears it.

sections.h: How Long Does Polymeric Sand Last?

blocks.p: A properly installed polymeric joint commonly lasts 3 to 10 years before it needs refreshing, and longer on sheltered patios with light foot traffic. Where you land in that range depends far more on installation and base than on the bag you bought.

ul: Joints filled shallower than the 1 to 1.5 inch minimum.
A base that heaves or settles, which cracks firm joints along their length.
Pressure washing with a narrow tip held close, which cuts into cured sand.
Fine paver sand used in joints wider than its rating.
Heavy freeze-thaw cycles on poorly drained soil.

blocks.p: Sweep debris off the joints so seeds have nowhere to sprout, use a wide fan tip or a [surface cleaner attachment](/best-surface-cleaner-for-pressure-washer/) when you wash, and seal the pavers once the sand has fully cured. Follow the longer of the sand and sealer waiting times; makers range from a day or two to several weeks.

Joints dropping below the paver edge, crumbling sections and weeds rooting more often are the signs. New polymeric sand does not bond well to old cured sand, so remove the old material to full depth and reinstall rather than topping up. For a full look at what the product does and does not do over its life, see our [polymeric sand pros and cons](/polymeric-sand-pros-and-cons/).

sections.h: Is Polymeric Sand Safe for Pets, Plants and Grass?

blocks.p: Once cured, polymeric sand is generally considered inert and safe around pets and nearby plants. The risk sits in the installation day, not the years after.

Like most sand products, polymeric sand contains crystalline silica, and the fine dust raised by pouring, sweeping and blowing is the part you breathe. Wear a mask rated N95 or better, plus gloves and eye protection, and keep children and pets inside until the surface is clean and watered.
Uncured binder washing off the surface can leave a film on whatever it lands on. Rinse runoff toward the lawn rather than vegetable beds as a precaution, and follow the bag's disposal notes.

Polymeric sand is not a herbicide. It stops weeds rooting through the joint and makes the surface too hard for most seeds, but wind-blown seeds can still sprout in debris that settles on top. Sweep regularly, pull the occasional shallow weed, and if you already have an established weed problem, clear it before installing; our [weed killer guide](/best-weed-killer/) covers options for paver joints.

mistakes: Shopping by brand instead of joint width

The best paver sand in the world will crack in a 2-inch flagstone gap, and a coarse stone binder will not pack into a 1/8-inch paver joint. Measure your narrowest and widest joints first and buy only a product whose printed range covers them. If one project mixes both, plan on two products.
Spreading on pavers that only look dry

After pressure washing, the surface can look dry in hours while the bottom of the joints stays damp for days. That hidden moisture activates binder on contact and smears it across the faces. Wait at least a full dry day, longer in shade or humidity, and check a few shady joints with a fingertip.
Leaving dust in textured paver faces

A broom alone leaves fine dust in tumbled and textured surfaces, and that dust turns into a polymer film the moment water hits it. Follow the broom with a leaf blower held almost flat, then look across the patio toward the light. Any faint sheen means another pass before watering.
Flooding the joints to finish faster

A hose on full flow fills joints faster than they can absorb, lifting binder and fines up and over the paver edges. Use a shower setting, mist in short passes and let each soak in before the next, following the exact count on your bag. Water should disappear into the joints, not run across the surface.
Topping up failed joints with new sand

Fresh polymeric sand does not bond to old cured sand, so a thin layer poured over a crumbly or washed-out joint breaks loose within a season. Dig the old sand out to full depth with a joint scraper, oscillating tool or angled pressure washer tip, let the joints dry and reinstall as if the patio were new.
bottomLine: For a standard concrete or clay paver patio, Alliance Gator Maxx G2 is the safest all-round polymeric sand: easy to find, forgiving and offered in the colors most pavers need. Spend more on Techniseal HP NextGel when your pavers are smooth, light or sealed and haze would be hard to live with, and skip paver sand entirely for flagstone in favor of GatorDust or Techniseal RG+. DOMINATOR suits homes far from a supplier, and PowerLoc covers small budget jobs if you follow its watering steps to the letter. Whatever you buy, the installation decides the result: measure the joints, start on dry pavers with a dry forecast, clean the surface completely and mist patiently.

faqs.q: What is the best polymeric sand on the market?
faqs.a: For most paver patios, Alliance Gator Maxx G2 is the best polymeric sand because it is widely stocked, forgiving and available in common paver colors. Techniseal HP NextGel is the better pick for smooth, light or sealed pavers where haze would show. For flagstone, the best choices are wide-joint binders such as Alliance GatorDust or Techniseal RG+.

faqs.q: What is the best polymeric sand for flagstone?
faqs.a: Alliance GatorDust is the best polymeric sand for flagstone, with Techniseal RG+ a close alternative. Both are coarse wide-joint binders whose labels run to several inches of joint width, so they bridge flagstone gaps without splitting down the middle. Check the maximum width and minimum depth on the bag, and buy extra, because wide joints use material quickly.

faqs.q: Which polymeric sand is better, DOMINATOR or Techniseal?
faqs.a: Both work well in paver joints when installed on dry pavers with careful misting. Techniseal HP NextGel is the stronger pick for smooth or light pavers because its gel binder is built to reduce haze, and it is sold through landscape suppliers. DOMINATOR makes more sense if no supplier is nearby, since it ships to the door, but compare the per-pound cost after shipping.

faqs.q: Can I use paver polymeric sand in wide joints?
faqs.a: Only up to the maximum width printed on the bag, which for most fine paver sands is roughly 1/2 inch to 1 inch. Wider than that, fine sand tends to shrink, crack along the center and wash out. Use a wide-joint binder for the wide sections and keep the two products separated by a border or a change in surface.

faqs.q: How deep should polymeric sand joints be?
faqs.a: Most makers want at least 1 to 1.5 inches of polymeric sand in the joint, and many recommend filling the full depth of the paver. Shallower joints do not hold enough binder, so they crack and lift. Clean old sand out to that depth before installing, and stop the fill about 1/8 inch below the paver surface or just under the chamfer.

faqs.q: Is all polymeric sand the same quality?
faqs.a: No. Products differ in joint width range, how forgiving the binder is during watering, how much haze it tends to leave and how firm the cured joint feels. Premium gel-type sands are more tolerant of small mistakes, while budget bags often punish over-watering. The biggest difference, though, is fit: a sand rated for your joint width matters more than the brand.

faqs.q: Does polymeric sand stop all weeds?
faqs.a: No. Polymeric sand stops most weeds from rooting through the joint and makes the surface too hard for seeds to settle easily, but wind-blown seeds can still sprout in dust and leaves that collect on top. Regular sweeping keeps that to a minimum. It is far better than plain sand against weeds, but it is low maintenance rather than no maintenance.
